children: By Patti Domm

Savant Wealth Management CEO Brent Brodeski says merging with other firms has been a powerful strategy that has helped Savant grow faster than he expected, find top talent, and provide one-stop shopping for clients looking for services such as tax and accounting advice.

It has also been a path that allowed Savant to grow in specialty niches. For example, Savant has built expertise in advising clients who teach at universities. It also has a team focused on helping ultrahigh-net-worth women going through divorce. And in 2024, it acquired another firm that specializes in serving the elderly.

Ten years ago, Brodeski set a goal "to improve a million lives," he says. "I think we're going to get there in about five years, give or take." Brodeski estimates that Savant now affects 269,000 people directly or indirectly, meaning clients, employees, and its local communities.

The advisory firm ranks 21st on Barron's 2026 Top 100 RIA F irms and has about $56 billion in assets under management. Barron's recently spoke with Brodeski, along with Zach Ivey, chief investment and advice officer, and Kevin Hrdlicka, head of wealth, about Savant's growth strategy, structure, and investment approach. An edited version of the conversation follows.

Barron's: Brent, you've been leading this firm since the 1980s, and you've seen a tremendous amount of growth through mergers and acquisitions. I'm wondering whether that is a strategy you will continue.

Brent Brodeski: It is really a strategy to reinforce organic growth. The best way to grow is a client at a time. The challenge with just trying to grow organically is that it's hard to really expand the footprint. Zach and his team in Birmingham, Ala., joined us two and a half years ago, and I couldn't have hired them, but I could partner with them. And now Zach is our chief advice and investment officer.
What a great way to get talent. I look around our organization: Whether it's our top advisors, the top growing advisors, our leadership, our executives, almost all of them have come through M&A.

We started almost 40 years ago in Rockford, Ill. We became the big fish in a little bowl, and when we tried to just open greenfield offices [where there wasn't an existing office], it was really hard. If you open up a greenfield office somewhere-we did that in Peoria, Ill.; we did it in Madison, Wis.; we did it in the Chicago suburbs-the phone doesn't start ringing because you don't know people, you don't have referral sources, you don't know the communities. So, we realized we needed to actually go to places like Birmingham-where Zach and his team were very established, knew the community, and had a great client base-and then bring them in, and then grow together faster than they could on their own or we could on our own.

When you get in certain markets-like, we're in Los Angeles now and New York now-you plant the flag, but you're a drop in the bucket. But once we have a flag, it's a lot easier to go and find other partners and to grow. We went from nothing in California; we'll probably have six or seven firms there. We had nothing in New York; we're probably going to have four or five within 12 months. Being able to create density allows us to organically grow faster in the markets we've chosen.

We're organically growing over 8% a year, without being in the custodial referral programs in a big way. That's significant. But there are plays out there we don't have. Things like niche playbooks. Sometimes when we partner, they might have a better play in their book than we do.
What do you mean by niches?

Brodeski: An example: We are probably the biggest niche provider for tenured university professors in the Big Ten and Ivy Leagues. It's an interesting niche. These people are wired differently, and they have different needs.

Another one would be C-suite level executives at publicly traded companies. We have a firm that specializes in exit planning for businesses. We have a firm in New York City that works with ultrahigh-net-worth divorced women. We just closed yesterday on an accounting firm, and all they do is physicians and dentists. They're excited about now being able to introduce financial planning, investments, wealth transfer, and retirement plans because they've got these clients who need these things, and they see them getting poorly served by other advisors. Now that creates a medical niche.

We have our accounting firm. We have 175 professionals. That brings us deep experience being able to help business owners not only with their businesses, but with their personal wealth. And then when they sell their business, someday our family office division can help them manage money and take over administrative responsibility.

I want to mention a firm we acquired in Kentucky; they built their entire company around longevity. They're experts on gerontology and end-of-life issues. Our clients, on average, are old. Our clients often have health issues, or their parents have end-of-life issues. That is expertise that we didn't have, but our whole organization, all of our advisors, could benefit from that wisdom and that knowledge of how to bring peace of mind and comfort to that last stage of life, whether it's the parents or the actual clients.
How have these mergers affected your clients?

Kevin Hrdlicka: With all of the M&A, what ends up happening is you have to get really good at training new advisors. In many cases, they've been doing this 30 years, and they have a way of doing it. Well, now they join Savant, and we have a team of tax strategists that can do a client's tax return.

We want to own the whole financial experience for a client. We believe that leads to much better advice. So, we train them that when you onboard a client, let's get their tax return, let's give a tax strategy update as part of the traditional financial plan. Embedding tax with investments is something that our clients want. When we get a new client, that is the top reason they pick Savant.
Zach, Why don't you jump in here. Bond yields are rising to levels that we haven't seen in a few years. How is that affecting your investment advice at this point?

Zach Ivey: Well, we espouse an evidence-based approach to investing. We don't really believe that investors get paid to predict the future, and we shouldn't be doing that, either. We get paid for bearing risk in a kind of disciplined way, and that simply means very thoughtful diversification.

On the stock side of things, we use a factor-based approach to breaking up the equity markets, and on the bond side, we likewise favor a very diversified portfolio. That protects you for all the different things that could happen. This approach seems really timely today, but we've been doing it a long time.
Are you viewing bonds as the ballast in your portfolio, and is this move in interest rates affecting that?
Ivey: Bonds are our liquidity and ballast to the portfolio, although for some investors, we do utilize alternative investments, which are often a risk reducer but without all that interest-rate risk.
What type of alternative investments are you looking at?

Ivey: We often think about alternatives not as one particular thing, but really as a recipe. So, we use asset classes like real assets, farmland, timberland, infrastructure, some diversified strategies like hedge funds, as well as trend following, private credit, reinsurance. Some of these, if you think of them individually, you would say, "Wow, that is a unique asset." But when we blend them together, they really can do a lot to accomplish that diversification in the portfolio.

In most cases, when we're utilizing alternatives-and not all investors have alternatives-we start allocations at around 10% and go up to around 20% in alternatives. A lot of that is coming off the bond side of the portfolio.
Brent, what other niches are you looking at?

Brodeski: We aren't in the airline pilot niche, and I would love to be. Most of them are coming through the military, and they've got a certain sort of persona. They can work with any generic advisor, but an advisor that really understands pilots is going to be able to create better alignment and more comfortable, better advice.
Thanks, Brent, Zach, and Kevin.
